newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil and Argentina spar over U.N. reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil and Argentina spar over U.N. reform.

text.p: A long-simmering rivalry between Brazil and Argentina flared up on Tuesday in a clash over who should represent South America on the United Nations Security Council should it one day be expanded.
Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia blasted Argentine President Carlos Menem for criticizing Brasilia's bid for a permanent seat on the council, officials said.
"Menem's remarks were received here by us with surprise and displeasure," Lampreia said on Monday night, according to a Foreign Ministry spokesman.
"They (the remarks) represent a true veto, which we cannot accept and which does not fit in with the central notion that there exists a strategic alliance between Brazil and Argentina," he said.
Argentine embassy officials were not available to comment.
Buenos Aires and its giant northern neighbor have for decades sparred over regional influence.
The establishment in 1995 of the Mercosur customs union, which in addition to Brazil and Argentina groups Uruguay and Paraguay, partly laid to rest that rivalry.

But Brazil, the world's fifth most populous country and among its top 10 economies, is finding its feet in the global community and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso feels it is ready to take on more responsibility internationally.
Brasilia's campaign for a permanent seat should the Security Council be expanded has been low-key but persistent.
Menem criticized Brazil's U.N. ambitions in a weekend interview with the O Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper, warning it would "break the balance we currently have in the region."
The Argentine leader has called for a rotating seat to be shared by countries in South America.
Lampreia said Menem had spoken out of turn.
"We want to ensure that this issue of the Security Council does not create a division or deep dissension between Brazil and Argentina," he said.
Presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral on Monday night also expressed Cardoso's "surprise," saying had it been the other way round, Argentina would have had Brazil's support.
Argentina, one of the world's richest countries at the turn of the century but now suffering from poverty and high unemployment, periodically lashes out at Brazil.
In the past two year, Buenos Aires fretted over Brazilian car industry rules which encourage investment and over retrictions on import financing that hurt Argentine exports.
Brazilians generally raise their eyebrows at the temper tantrums of their southern neighbors.
But Cardoso has made bilateral relations a priority and his strong personal friendship with Menem has so far managed to brush all controversies under the carpet.
